scenes.title: Is everything AI now?
scenes.description: Daniel, a receptionist, starts his day at a busy company. A colleague says AI helps with almost everything now. Four tools on his desk light up: a calendar, a check-in tablet, a shared inbox and a badge printer.
lines: Daniel is a receptionist at a busy company.
Every morning, he welcomes visitors, answers questions, books appointments and makes sure everyone gets to the right place.
This week, the company introduced some new digital tools.
A colleague leans over the desk and says, “Daniel, we’ve got AI helping with almost everything now!”
Daniel looks at his screen and wonders: does that mean everything on here is AI?
Not quite.
Let’s look at the tools Daniel uses today, and how each one actually works.

scenes.title: The appointment reminder
scenes.description: Daniel books a 2 pm appointment with a reminder fifteen minutes before. The clock moves forward and the reminder appears at 1:45. The rule behind it is shown: fifteen minutes before an appointment, show a reminder.
lines: A visitor is coming in at two o’clock.
Daniel books the appointment and sets a reminder for fifteen minutes before.
At quarter to two, the reminder pops up, right on time.
Useful?
Definitely.
But the system doesn’t need AI to do that.
Someone wrote a clear instruction: fifteen minutes before an appointment, show a reminder.
The software follows that instruction exactly, every time.
It doesn’t learn, guess or predict.
That’s ordinary software doing what it was programmed to do.

scenes.title: The visitor check-in
scenes.description: A visitor types her name and host on a reception tablet. Three steps light up in order: save the details, print a badge, notify the host.
lines: At two o’clock, the visitor arrives.
Instead of filling in a paper form, she types her name and who she’s meeting on a tablet.
The system records her arrival, prints a badge and sends a message to her host.
It all happens automatically, and it looks quite clever.
But each step is an instruction someone set up in advance: save the details, print the badge, send the message.
Automatic doesn’t mean AI.
A system can collect information, store it and follow steps without any artificial intelligence at all.

scenes.title: The smart inbox
scenes.description: Sorted example messages, with shared words highlighted, train a tool. A new message arrives and the tool suggests a folder based on the patterns it learned.
lines: Next, Daniel opens the shared reception inbox.
There are messages about parking, deliveries, meeting rooms and visitor access.
The company has a new tool that suggests where each message should go.
This one works differently.
Nobody wrote a rule for every possible message.
Instead, the tool was trained on hundreds of messages that people had already sorted.
It learned patterns, such as which words tend to appear in parking questions, and uses them to predict where a new message belongs.
That’s machine learning, one way of building AI.
And because it’s a prediction, it won’t always be right.

scenes.title: When the prediction is wrong
scenes.description: A message saying the check-in tablet is not working is filed under Visitor Information because of the words visitor and check-in. Daniel reads it and moves it to IT Support.
lines: Then Daniel spots something.
A message says, “The visitor check-in tablet isn’t working.”
The tool has put it under Visitor Information.
Why?
Probably because the message mentions “visitor” and “check-in”, words that often appear in visitor questions.
But Daniel reads the whole message.
Someone is reporting a broken device, so he moves it to IT Support.
The tool matched patterns in the words.
Daniel understood what the person actually needed.
That’s why predictions like this still need a human check.

scenes.title: So what's the difference?
scenes.description: Two columns compare tools that follow instructions with a tool that learns patterns. A card for rule-based expert systems from Lesson 3 joins the AI side. A closing question asks what a system does and how it works.
lines: So, what did Daniel’s day show us?
The reminder and the check-in system follow instructions that people wrote.
They’re useful, automatic and reliable, and they don’t need AI.
The smart inbox learned patterns from examples and makes predictions.
That’s one way AI can work.
But here’s a twist.
Remember the expert systems from Lesson 3?
Some AI uses rules too, written down from experts’ knowledge to make judgments.
So the real question is what a system does and how it decides.
Next time someone says a tool uses AI, don’t just go by the label.
Ask: what does it actually do, and how does it work?
Something can be automatic, helpful and impressive without being AI.
